text:
Recent work supports separating temporal sensitivity from useful temporal prediction. [CETRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03047) distinguishes absolute recency from relative order through counterfactual tuning, although its evidence concerns LLM recommenders rather than BERT4Rec. [Diagnosing and Mitigating Mid-Sequence Degradation (SIGIR 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805712.3809738) reports boundary-focused attention persisting when informative collaborative signals move, suggesting architectural position bias beyond positional embeddings. Neither establishes temporal shortcut learning in the supplied model.

[BERT4Rec’s original formulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) uses masked-item supervision to prevent target leakage through bidirectional context. A practical diagnostic synthesis: preserve history length, item multiset, padding and fixed candidates while shuffling older items with the latest item anchored; separately swap recent and distant items to test recency assignment. Intervene on position IDs while keeping token order fixed to probe absolute-position dependence, treating this as an out-of-distribution stress test. Use frequency-matched identity replacements as a separate content control; deletion alone conflates content, length and position.

For the existing single model, measure paired changes in target rank, target-versus-negative margins and HR@10, then confirm effects on user-disjoint public training prefixes. Proposed mechanistic follow-up: restore clean activations in individual attention blocks during corrupted-history runs and test whether ranking recovers; attention weights alone cannot establish causal contribution. Keep appended-MASK inference and final nonpadding readout throughout. These are diagnostic proposals inferred from the literature, requiring no auxiliary scorer, additional checkpoint or score fusion.
